prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The starting network never placed a brick: it learned to choose DONE straight away, and episode length had already fallen to 1.7 by 25% of training. The traces show why. The target heights the agent sees are not the real design: each row is shifted around by X/2 columns (on 8x8, the left and right halves swap; rows stay put). The rewards in the untrained trace match the real design, not the observed one. So the observed target channels, and possibly the missing/extra channels, don't line up with the build or with the action grid. A local 1x1/3x3 network can't connect "this cell is missing" with "place a brick here", every placement looks random and loses reward, and DONE (reward 0) wins. The fix should be to feed the network both the raw input and a copy shifted by X/2, so whichever version is correctly aligned is available. This is only slicing and concatenating before the first learned layer, which the rules allow. After that, the anti-collapse recipe and network capacity are tested one change at a time.

### Round 2
The shifted-input fix is what made learning possible. The best trial, r1c2 (2 PPO epochs, entropy 0.02, about 225k steps), scored 0.63. The default recipe (r1c1) scored 0.59. The two seeds of each differ by about 0.25, so these two cannot be told apart. The wider trunk (r1c3) got about 40% fewer steps and fell to 0.28, so the number of samples seems to matter. Training success was still rising at the end of every run. In both diagnostic traces, the agent fills the low cells and then picks DONE. It leaves out tall stacks and overhangs, such as a 1x2 brick that should land at layer 2 resting on a 2-high column. To place those, the network must find the landing layer (the highest filled cell under the footprint) and then check the target at that layer. A trunk that sees each column as a whole does this poorly. Next: a placement head that scores each layer separately, more samples by using 1 PPO epoch, and longer credit assignment.

### Round 3
The observed target is rolled X/2 columns. Feeding a rolled copy of the input fixed the collapse to DONE (0 → about 0.6). Seed spread is large: one seed pair gave 0.49 and 0.77, so I treat ±0.15 as noise. The recipe matters a lot. 2 PPO epochs (0.63) beat 4 epochs (0.59). 1 epoch dropped to 0.08: it plateaued early and leaned on 1x1 bricks. gamma 0.99 dropped to 0.11 and was slow to escape early DONE. A wider trunk with a global bias (0.28) and the per-layer head (0.29) cost steps and did not help. Every run loses the first 25% or more of training to the DONE collapse. Greedy traces fail on upper-layer overhangs: the agent picks DONE even when the right overhang brick could be placed. So the head does not combine the landing layer with whether the target cell at that layer is wanted. This round tests a richer footprint head and two one-change recipe tweaks: more gradient steps per sample, and higher entropy.

### Round 4
Every observed target is shifted by X/2 columns. Rolling the input to undo that shift is what took dev success from 0 to about 0.6 (r1c1, r1c2). After that, the recipe mattered more than the architecture. Doubling the minibatches from 16 to 32 raised the score from 0.63 to 0.89 (r3c2, both seeds above 0.85), which is well beyond the seed spread. Raising entropy from 0.02 to 0.04 at 16 minibatches gave 0.74, a likely gain of about 0.1. Changes that made the network wider or the head more complex scored worse (r1c3, r2c1, r3c1). Using 1 PPO epoch or a longer horizon hurt badly (r2c2, r2c3). So the limit is gradient steps per sample plus early exploration, not network capacity. The remaining failures are wrong upper-layer bricks on tall stacks and early DONE, and training success was still rising at the end. This last round keeps the r3c2 network and tests: 64 minibatches alone, entropy 0.04 at 32 minibatches, and both together.

## Trial it ended with
name: best net, 64 minibatches
hypothesis: Same as r3c2, but with 64 minibatches of 64 samples instead of 32 of 128. That doubles the gradient steps per update again while the sample count stays near 225k. Going from 16 to 32 minibatches raised dev success from 0.63 to 0.89, and training success was still rising, so gradient steps still seem to be the limit. Refuted if the 2-seed dev mean falls below about 0.85.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 1 says the observed target is shifted with wraparound along x: "each row is shifted around by X/2 columns (on 8x8, the left and right halves swap; rows stay put)". It adds that "the observed target channels, and possibly the missing/extra channels" are misaligned. On an 8-wide grid that is the 4-column wrapped roll. Rounds 3–4 repeat it: "The observed target is rolled X/2 columns." Caveat: "X/2" would differ from a fixed 4 columns on grids that aren't 8 wide.
